City of Hope: real-time sepsis prediction for bone marrow transplant patients

How one of the largest cancer centers in the US uses Kafka and Confluent Cloud to feed AI models with live clinical data.

Context

City of Hope is one of the largest cancer research and treatment organizations in the United States. It builds its own AI models to predict events during treatment, including a sepsis risk model for bone marrow transplant patients, whose immune systems are temporarily compromised.

The problem

In a clinical setting, a prediction only has value if it arrives in time for the team to act. Models fed with batch-consolidated data warn too late, and sepsis progresses fast.

The solution

The Epic electronic health record generates HL7 messages in real time on every change, such as a new lab result or a new blood pressure reading. Those messages land in Kafka topics, go through microservices that check conditions and store information, and trigger the model to produce a prediction. The platform runs on Confluent Cloud on Microsoft Azure, and connectors made it possible to link the data to Kafka in a couple of hours.

Results

According to Confluent, the sepsis prediction model reduces sepsis and ICU escalation rates among bone marrow transplant patients. The case does not publish percentages.

What this means for your team

Hospitals and health insurers start from the same place: health records that already emit HL7 or FHIR events, and models that run on yesterday’s data. City of Hope’s gain did not come from a new model but from delivering the data to the model the moment it changes. Under privacy regulation, the design needs masking and access control in the flow itself.
